newsitem.title: USA: Miami Beach cops feel heat from Versace saga.
newsitem.headline: Miami Beach cops feel heat from Versace saga.

text.p: Instead of celebrating its success in tracking down suspected murderer Andrew Cunanan, Miami Beach police are mired in dispute and despondency.

The department's now-dismissed spokesman says he has become a scapegoat, a SWAT unit threatened to resign after missing out on the action, and its chief is fending off criticism about its performance in the hunt for Cunanan, the suspected killer of fashion designer Gianni Versace.

"Morale is very low because we feel we did a pretty good job," Bobby Hernandez, another spokesman, said Friday. "Cunanan ran across the country before he got here. We kept him within 40 blocks of the (Versace) murder and we got him."

Versace was shot outside his Ocean Drive mansion on July 15, an act which thrust local police into the world spotlight. Cunanan, a gay prostitute posted on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted List over four other murders, was named as the only suspect.
Eight days later, acting on a caretaker's tip, police stormed a houseboat less than three miles away. Inside they found Cunanan's corpse. He had committed suicide.
Police spokesman Al Boza first told reporters no body had been found on the boat, and it was several hours before the correct information was given.
The next day Police Chief Richard Barreto publicly apologised. But Boza, a popular figure who for a week had kept a news-hungry world informed with unfailing politeness, was relieved of his job.
"I feel like I'm the scapegoat. I'm the fall guy in this whole thing," he told reporters before taking off on holiday.
His mistake was to interpret the SWAT team's "all clear" message as meaning there was no body when in fact it meant the houseboat was safe for police.

"This man is highly respected and he has been caught in this situation because the chief failed to take responsibilty for the breakdown and instead blamed Boza," Gus Sanchez, vice president of the Fraternal Order of Police union, said.

The Miami Beach police SWAT unit is also upset. They have threatened to resign because a team from Metro-Dade police, a county-wide force, was deployed instead. In a letter to City Manager Jose Garcia Pedroso, they said they had been "nationally embarrassed" by the decision.
After meeting with officials Thursday, the 17-man team put their resignations on hold pending further talks next week.
Hernandez suggested politics were behind the turmoil at police headquarters, which is just two blocks from Versace's home.
"This is what happens when things get mixed up with political agendas," he said. "We have contract negotiations next year so this might have something to do with it."

The SWAT team was not used because its main task was issuing warrants, Miami Beach Mayor Seymour Gelber said. After an earlier labour dispute, city officials decided an elite tactical unit was not needed in Miami Beach and the county squad would be called in if one was needed, he said.

The department is also facing questions about whether Cunanan could have been arrested before the murder. With four police agencies involved -- Miami Beach police, Metro-Dade police, the FBI and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement -- a certain amount of mutual fingerpointing has taken place.
Gelber defended the police in an open letter, saying that although mistakes were made they got the job done.

"The law enforcement agencies did what they are designed to do. Capture the criminal. No neatly bound television script, no Sherlock Holmes. No perfectly synchronized performance. They just did their job."
